newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-LEYLAND HEADED FOR MARLINS MANAGER POST.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-LEYLAND HEADED FOR MARLINS MANAGER POST.

text.p: The Florida Marlins appear to have won the Jim Leyland sweepstakes.

The National League Marlins have scheduled a news conference for later on Friday at which they are expected to announce that former Pittsburgh Pirates skipper Leyland will be the team's manager next season.
The California Angels, Chicago White Sox and Boston Red Sox had all sought the services of Leyland, who decided to leave the cost conscious Pirates at the end of this season.
The signing of Leyland would be another coup for Marlins owner Wayne Huizenga, who also landed highly-prized NFL coach Jimmy Johnson to run his Miami Dolphins this year.

"...barring a shocking change of heart, Leyland will be wearing a Marlins cap this morning, joining Jimmy Johnson of the Dolphins and Pat Riley of the (NBA) Heat as big names who have cast their lots with South Florida teams," the Fort Lauderdale Sun-Sentinel said in Friday's editions.
The Marlins fired manager Rene Lachemann in July and named John Boles as the second manager in the club's history. Florida was 40-35 under Boles and finished 80-82 overall in 1996.

Leyland led the Pirates to three consecutive National League East titles from 1990 to 1992, but became frustrated by management's cost-cutting in recent years, which saw the departure of such established stars as Bobby Bonilla, Barry Bonds and Doug Drabek.
The final straw may have come late last month, when the Pirates traded ace left-hander Denny Neagle in August to the pitching-rich Atlanta Braves in exchange for more young prospects.

The Pirates finished in last-place in the Central Division with a 73-89 record this season. During the 1996 campaign, the Pirates used 21 pitchers, many of them rookies whom Leyland said were not ready to pitch in the major leagues.

The 51-year-old Leyland managed the Pirates since 1986, posting an 849-860 record in 11 years. But he decided he had to make a move to a team with an owner willing to spend money on talent for a legitimate run at a championship.
